finding.claim: DELETE /files/<fid> deletes any file for any caller, including requests with no identity header, because the authorization check never denies anything.
finding.source: Any HTTP DELETE to /files/<fid>; g.user is None when the header is absent, otherwise any attacker-chosen value (views.py:12).

trace.note: require_allowed is bound to acl.is_allowed, not ensure_allowed
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') discards the boolean return value
is_allowed returns a bool and never calls abort

finding.guards_checked: acl.py:10 abort(403) exists only in ensure_allowed, which delete_file never calls. views.py:10-12 before_request sets g.user without authenticating. acl.py:5 fail-closed default is irrelevant because the result is ignored.
finding.repro: curl -X DELETE http://host/files/<existing-id> with no headers returns {"ok": true} and removes the entry. Not executed; established by reading the code.

verdict.guard_found: none effective. acl.py:10 abort(403) lives only in ensure_allowed, which views.py:26 uses but delete_file (views.py:15-20) never calls. views.py:18 imports is_allowed as require_allowed (views.py:4) and discards its bool return. acl.py:5 returns False for g.user=None, but nothing tests that value. views.py:11-12 before_request only copies the X-Session-User-Verified header into g.user with no authentication.
verdict.reason: The attacker is anonymous: views.py:18 calls is_allowed (acl.py:4-5), which returns a bool that is discarded, so views.py:19 `del STORE[fid]` runs for any request, including one with no header (g.user is None per views.py:12).

finding.claim: Caller identity comes from a client-supplied header with no verification in the app, so any caller can impersonate any principal that holds grants. Depends on deployment: exploitable if the app is reachable without a proxy that overwrites the header.
finding.source: HTTP header X-Session-User-Verified, fully attacker-controlled when the app is reachable directly.
finding.sink: g.user used for every authorization decision (views.py:18, views.py:26 via acl.py:5).
finding.guards_checked: No signature, session, or token validation in this code. The header name implies an upstream proxy sets it, but nothing here enforces that the header is stripped or overwritten at the edge.
finding.repro: With direct reachability, send X-Session-User-Verified: <user-with-grants> to act as that user. Not executed.

verdict.guard_found: None validate the header: views.py:10-12 copies X-Session-User-Verified into g.user with no signature, session, or proxy check. The authorization checks are is_allowed (acl.py:4-5), which returns a bool, and ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10), which aborts with 403. At views.py:18, require_allowed(...) is a bare call whose bool result is discarded, so delete_file has no effective check. At views.py:26, ensure_allowed does abort on failure, so rename_file is gated by whatever identity the header supplies.
verdict.reason: The trace lines exist as described (views.py:12, views.py:18, views.py:26, acl.py:5), and nothing in the code validates the header (views.py:12), but whether an attacker can reach the app without a header-overwriting proxy is a deployment fact the code cannot show. The candidate also misses that views.py:18 discards is_allowed's result, so DELETE has no authorization at all in the code, regardless of the header (acl.py:4-5).

finding.claim: Lookups occur before authorization. A missing fid raises an unhandled KeyError (500), while an existing file the caller cannot write to returns 403 on rename, giving an existence oracle.
finding.source: Any caller, via the fid path parameter.

trace.note: ensure_allowed aborts 403 only for existing files

finding.guards_checked: STORE is an in-memory dict with no tenant scoping; no error handler is registered.

verdict.guard_found: No guard precedes the lookup: before_request (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user from a header, and no error handler is registered anywhere in views.py. The only authorization on the rename path, ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10), runs after STORE[fid] at views.py:25 and aborts 403 correctly, so it cannot prevent the KeyError. The delete path's require_allowed is the bool-returning is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) with its result discarded at views.py:18, so it enforces nothing.
verdict.reason: The lookup at views.py:25 runs before ensure_allowed at views.py:26, so a missing fid gives an unhandled KeyError (500) while an existing file the caller cannot write to gets abort(403) from acl.py:10, which is a real existence oracle reachable by any caller who can hit the endpoint. The claim is accurate, though the more serious defect is that views.py:18 discards is_allowed's bool, so DELETE is not authorized at all.
